person.positioning: Moeein Aali is a full-stack software engineer at Yektanet who builds production systems end to end — from the React and Next.js frontend he goes deepest in, through the Django and Go services behind them, to the Kubernetes pipelines that ship them.
about: I'm a Computer Engineering student at Sharif University of Technology and a software engineer at Yektanet, where I've shipped interactive ad platforms, real-time analytics services, and the admin tooling that runs them. My depth is frontend — React and Next.js architecture, state and data-fetching design, and interfaces that stay fast under real traffic — but I've never wanted the job to stop at the browser.

That's meant writing Django and Nest.js services, a Socket.io analytics pipeline handling over a thousand requests a second, a Go crawler, and the Docker and CI/CD that deploy them. Alongside the industry work I've been a teaching assistant for more than twenty courses at Sharif, five of them as Head TA — which is where I learned that explaining a system clearly and designing one well are close to the same skill.

projects.title: ASIS Badges
projects.summary: Three bilingual Next.js sites for ASIS hardware-CTF badges — Iran Badge, YUZ Badge, and the umbrella landing at badge.asis.sh — with scroll-scrubbed 3D board assembly, interactive hardware specs, challenge catalogues, and live scoreboards.
highlights: Scroll-scrubbed explode→assemble GLB clip — sticky stage, rAF seek path outside React, frame-rate-independent easing
Specs page with a second model scene — orbit controls, annotated hotspots, and bilingual hardware tables
Mobile/desktop render profiles that drop transmission and contact shadows so a mid-range phone can scrub without stalling
One shared chassis across three live sites — fa/en RTL, dark-first UI, Docker + GHCR CI deploy
projects.body_md:
## Overview

ASIS Badges is one programme with three public frontends. Each edition of the
hardware CTF ships a custom PCB competitors wear and attack; each edition also
ships a site that tells the board's story, walks through assembly in 3D, lists
challenges, and shows the live scoreboard. The umbrella page at
[badge.asis.sh](https://badge.asis.sh) ties the editions into one family.

| Edition | Year | Badge | Site |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1st | 2024 | Iran Badge | [iran.badge.asis.sh](https://iran.badge.asis.sh) |
| 2nd | 2025 | YUZ Badge | [yuz.badge.asis.sh](https://yuz.badge.asis.sh) |
| — | — | Collection landing | [badge.asis.sh](https://badge.asis.sh) |

A third board (Damavand) is in design; the landing already reserves its slot.

## Scroll-scrubbed 3D assembly

The centrepiece of each edition site is not a play button — it is a scroll
runway. A tall section pins a sticky stage under the fixed header while
`window.scrollY` maps continuously onto a GLB explode→assemble clip inside
Google's `model-viewer`. Progress is 0 when the stage locks and 1 when the
section ends, so the visitor *assembles* the badge by scrolling.

The scrub path never goes through React state. Driving `setState` from scroll
would re-render the viewer tree every frame and force layout reads on top of
WebGL work — enough to stall a mid-range phone past its frame budget. Instead
an imperative `BoardViewer` handle exposes `setProgress`, and a
`requestAnimationFrame` loop eases toward the target with frame-rate-independent
smoothing. Geometry is measured only on mount and resize; the frame loop is
pure arithmetic over scroll position. An `IntersectionObserver` starts and stops
the loop so idle sections do not burn GPU. `prefers-reduced-motion` snaps
straight to the assembled pose.

Camera and runway live in a single `site-config` scene object — orbit, FOV,
scroll runway (taller on desktop, shorter on phones), animation clip name —
so framing can be tuned without touching component code. Because
`model-viewer`'s field of view is vertical, a landscape board like YUZ would
clip left and right on a portrait phone even when it fits top-to-bottom. The
viewer tracks stage aspect and pulls the orbit radius back proportionally
(capped) so the silhouette stays inside the frame.

Scroll is not only for the board. Section titles use GSAP `SplitText` +
`ScrollTrigger`, loaded lazily so a cold 3G visit still sees readable headings
before the animation bundle arrives. Velocity-linked marquees on Motion sit
between sections as lighter scroll texture.

## Interactive specs in 3D

`/specs` is a second scene, not a screenshot of the first. A dedicated static
GLB ships already assembled with no animation clips, so nothing has to be parked
or seeked. Camera controls are on — orbit and zoom — and bilingual hotspots sit
on the mesh (`data-position` / `data-normal`) for the MCU, OLED, GNSS, cellular
SIM path, SPI flash, shift registers, buttons, and USB-C. Tapping a hotspot
opens a dialog with what the part is and why it matters as an attack surface —
the same language competitors use on the floor.

Below the model, tabbed tables cover overview, modules, interfaces, and
mechanical data so the 3D layer and the datasheet stay one page instead of two
disconnected artefacts.

## Performance as a design constraint

A scroll-scrubbed clip pays its render bill on every frame. These models carry
hundreds of materials; any visible `KHR_materials_transmission` forces three.js
to re-render the whole scene into a multisampled, mipmapped target, then draw
transmissive objects again backface-first. That cost is flattened after load —
on desktop too, not only mobile — because the affected parts read as opaque
plastic anyway. The mobile render profile also zeros contact-shadow intensity
so `model-viewer` never allocates the per-frame depth and blur passes a phone
barely resolves. Touch gesture ownership flips while scrubbing (`touch-action:
none`, camera controls off) so the page scroll owns the runway and the board
does not fight the finger.

## One chassis, three accents

Iran Badge leads with cobalt. YUZ Badge leads with brass. The umbrella landing
owns neither — its theme tokens sit near zero chroma so colour on the page comes
only from the badge accents it presents. That keeps the shell from competing
with the boards it introduces, and keeps the three sites readable as one family
rather than three unrelated marketing pages.

Under the paint, the stack is the same: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4,
shadcn/ui, bilingual Persian/English with proper RTL, dark-first theming, and
Docker images pushed to GHCR then deployed over SSH. Challenges, galleries, and
scoreboards round out each edition site; locale and theme switchers live in the
header so one build serves both audiences.

projects.title: Arcadia
projects.summary: A Steam-like digital game platform built as 14 event-driven microservices — publishing, wallet and gift cards, an item marketplace with a real order-matching engine, community, and a hybrid recommendation engine — deployed to Kubernetes with Prometheus, Grafana, and Loki observability.
highlights: 14 independently owned services, each with its own database and no cross-service joins
Financial correctness via Outbox + Saga + DLQ — exactly-once transfers, compensating rollbacks, an append-only ledger
An item marketplace with a real price-time-priority order-matching engine
A hybrid recommendation engine combining pgvector embeddings with collaborative filtering
Deployed to a k3s cluster with generated Grafana dashboards, Prometheus alerting, and Loki log correlation by request id
projects.body_md:
## Overview

Arcadia is a digital game distribution platform — a Steam-like store where
developers publish games, players buy and gift them from a wallet, an item
marketplace lets players trade in-game items against a live order book, and a
community layer wraps it all in reviews, posts, and festivals. It began as the
architecture project for a graduate microservices course, but the brief was
never "make it work" — it was "make it correct under failure," which is a
different and much harder assignment. It shipped as 14 independently deployed
services across a real Kubernetes cluster, with the observability stack
needed to actually operate it.

## Bounded contexts, enforced, not assumed

Fourteen services — Auth & Profile, Catalog, Order, Wallet, Payment,
Marketplace, Review, Community, Search, Recommendation, Media, Notification,
Festival, and the API Gateway — each own their domain outright: their own
database, their own deploy pipeline, their own on-call story. Database-per-
service is usually a diagram; here it is a guarantee enforced by Postgres
grants, not convention. `CONNECT` is revoked from `PUBLIC` on every database,
so the wallet service's role physically cannot open a connection to the
payment service's tables — exactly as true as if they ran on different hosts,
because a design that only *happens* to keep services from touching each
other's data is a design that will eventually be violated by someone in a
hurry.

## Money has to be exactly right, not usually right

A store that sells things needs its ledger to never drift, and distributed
transactions are exactly where that goes wrong first. A purchase is a saga:
order reserves the game, wallet holds the funds, payment settles, and if any
step fails the prior steps unwind through compensating transactions rather
than leaving the system in a half-completed state. Every write that must both
land in a database and announce itself on Kafka goes through the Outbox
pattern, so a crash between "committed" and "published" is impossible by
construction rather than merely unlikely. Messages that a consumer cannot
process do not vanish — every consumed topic has a dead-letter companion, and
the two command topics (`wallet-commands`, `catalog-commands`) dead-letter on
so much as an unrecognized message, because an addressed command a service
doesn't understand is a contract violation someone needs to see, not noise to
swallow. The reward split on every sale — 70% to the developer, 30% to the
platform — runs through the same guarantee, so "the money is right" is not a
property you check afterward with a script; it is a property the design
cannot violate.

## A marketplace with a real matching engine

Beyond buying published games, players trade in-game items directly: list an
item for sale or place a buy order, and the marketplace service runs actual
price-time-priority matching against a live order book — the same mechanism
that prices a stock exchange, scaled down to game items and required to clear
outstanding orders in seconds. It is a genuinely different problem from the
CRUD-shaped features around it, and it is treated as one: its own bounded
context, its own periodic matching job, its own failure mode that cannot be
allowed to touch the wallet ledger except through the same saga discipline as
everything else that moves money.

## Recommendations that combine two different signals

The recommendation service is a hybrid engine, not a single model bolted on
for a demo. It consumes `PurchaseCompleted`, `ReviewPosted`, and
`GamePublished` events to build two complementary views: a content-based
similarity model over game genre and tag embeddings, stored as `vector`
columns in a pgvector-enabled Postgres (the platform runs
`pgvector/pgvector:pg16` specifically because the stock image cannot open
this extension — a migration that fails silently there leaves the service
reporting healthy while every query against the new column errors), and
collaborative filtering over what similar players bought. Combining the two
is what makes "games like this one" and "players like you bought this" both
answerable from the same service instead of needing two.

## Making event-driven correctness legible

Fourteen services sharing a Kafka bus is only as maintainable as the map of
who talks to whom, so that map is written down and treated as a design
artifact, not tribal knowledge: the notification service deliberately does
not consume `wallet-events` (a balance change is not news to the person who
just spent the money — what's news is the order it paid for), and does not
read review or community events either, because a reported comment is
Support's concern and Support already sees it in the queue inside the service
that owns it. Getting an event's *consumers* right is as much a design
decision as getting its schema right, and it's the kind of decision that is
invisible until it's wrong.

## Running it for real

The platform deploys to a k3s cluster behind Traefik with cert-manager, each
service on its own autoscaler (the gateway floors at 3 replicas, domain
services at 1, both scaling to CPU), and an observability stack where the
dashboards are generated code: one Grafana dashboard per service plus an
overview, produced by a script that runs in CI so a dashboard cannot silently
drift from the metrics it queries. Logs correlate across all 14 services by a
single request id, so tracing one purchase across order, wallet, payment, and
notification is one Loki query, not four terminal tabs. A 123-check
end-to-end suite exercises the real workflows — a game published, bought,
refunded, and gifted; a marketplace trade matched under a genuine race; every
dead-letter queue confirmed empty; every ledger balance confirmed equal to
the sum of its own history — because five services once passed 389 green
unit tests and still produced nine bugs in the first hour the stack ran for
real, and every one of those nine was about configuration and topology, the
exact class of bug unit tests cannot see.

projects.title: Comeback
projects.summary: Built from scratch: a native-like Persian sports PWA proven at over one million users — WebSocket live chat and scores, AI comment moderation and news labeling on a cost-optimized model, an MCP server for agent-driven admin, automated Remotion match videos, and Bazel/Kubernetes delivery — shipped across TWA and Swift.
highlights: Built from scratch as an optimized native-like PWA serving 1M+ users
WebSocket live chat for real-time fan conversation during matches
WebSocket-driven live scores through peak-traffic match windows
Production delivery with Bazel, Kubernetes, and HPA autoscaling
Prometheus/Grafana monitoring for resilience under live-event load
Mobile delivery through TWA and Swift
AI comment moderation on Jev, a cost-optimized model that replaced a general-purpose LLM, with cost and per-category metrics
AI news labeling at about $0.00015 per article, powering sport and tag feeds in Redis
MCP server (Go, Keycloak OAuth) so editors run the admin panel from AI agents
Automated pre- and post-match Instagram story videos rendered with Remotion
Technical SEO overhaul: server-rendered pages, honest sitemaps, canonicals, Open Graph cards
projects.body_md:
## Overview

Comeback is an optimized native-like Persian sports platform built from
scratch that has served more than one million users. The application brings
together a sports news feed, WebSocket live chat, WebSocket-backed live match
scores, prediction flows, and personalized content in a single product. Its
mobile-first PWA is engineered to feel like a real app — installable, fast
under the thumb, and resilient during peak-traffic moments around live events.

## Product engineering

The frontend is built with Next.js, while Go services support the product's
backend integrations and delivery needs. Real-time surfaces — including
live chat and live scores / match-state updates — travel over WebSockets
so the UI stays current without polling during high-traffic games. The
product integrates the Yeklist public APIs for sports content and live
data, including separate client and server paths where they are
appropriate for the experience.

The work also includes the supporting application integrations: sports data,
authentication, push-notification preferences, analytics, and a Service Worker
for the installable PWA behavior expected on mobile. Mobile delivery covers a
Trusted Web Activity release that feels native on Android, plus Swift.

## Delivery and observability

Comeback is delivered on Kubernetes behind load balancing, with Bazel for
reproducible builds, Docker/OCI images, and HPA autoscaling to keep the
service resilient under peak traffic. Prometheus and Grafana provide the
monitoring surface for production health during live-event load. This
production architecture keeps the deployment path repeatable while allowing
the platform to scale with sports traffic at million-user volume.

## AI and cost optimization

Comeback uses AI where it is cheapest and most measurable. Comment
moderation moved from a general-purpose LLM prompt to Jev, Yektanet's
cost-optimized classification model: each policy category is a separate
yes/no probability question, severe bad words are caught by a deterministic
filter first, and a circuit breaker fails open so an AI outage never blocks
the chat. Prometheus tracks Jev cost, tokens, failure reasons, and per-category
scores, so spend is visible and thresholds can be tuned.

A Python cron job labels every crawled sports article with a sport, tags, and
an importance score using two Jev calls (about $0.00015 per article), under run
budgets, chunked commits, and a watchdog. The labels build pre-ranked Redis
feeds, so the news page filters by sport and tag, and high-importance stories
are posted to Telegram automatically.

## Automation and tooling

An MCP server in Go, protected by Keycloak OAuth with mandatory PKCE, token
introspection, and confirmation-gated, audited write tools, lets editors run
the admin panel from AI agents such as Claude Code. Comeback Studio uses
Remotion templates and a render worker to generate pre-match and post-match
Instagram story videos from live match data. A technical SEO pass added
server-rendered pages, indexable-only sitemaps, canonicals, and cached Open
Graph cards.

projects.title: Zerang
projects.summary: An AI study companion for Konkur students — RAG-grounded Q&A, an AI-generated study plan with a persistent counselor, and a native-like PWA plus TWA Android app on a Django/Next.js stack.
highlights: Course-scoped RAG chat over teacher-uploaded PDFs and voice notes, with async transcription
AI-generated 14-day study plans that a persistent AI counselor can revise through an explicit propose-then-apply flow
Native-like PWA with a custom Service Worker for installability and cache management
Parallel TWA Android release with FCM push and per-store in-app billing across Bazaar, Myket, and direct
projects.body_md:
## Overview

Zerang is an AI study companion built for Konkur — Iran's national university
entrance exam — where students spend a year working through a fixed set of
courses under real time pressure. The product's job is to sit inside that
year: answer questions grounded in what a teacher actually assigned, turn a
loose set of goals into a concrete two-week schedule, and keep nudging a
student back onto that schedule without ever pretending to have changed it
when it hasn't. I co-founded the product with the Sharif AI Products team and
owned the engineering end to end — architecture, web client, and Android
delivery — built as a production system rather than an MVP.

## Chat scoped to what was actually taught

The chat surface is not a general assistant bolted onto a login page. Teachers
create Classes and Sessions, upload PDFs and voice notes into each Session,
and students ask questions scoped to that material through a Retrieval-
Augmented Generation pipeline against an external RAG service. Voice notes are
chunked into five-minute segments and transcribed concurrently rather than as
one long blocking call, so a lecture recording becomes queryable text in
roughly the time it takes to upload it. There are three separate streaming
chat surfaces — course-scoped chat, session chat, and general/exam-review chat
— each backed by Server-Sent Events, because course-scoped chat is the
majority of real student traffic and treating it as a special case of a
generic "chat" endpoint would have made it too easy to add a feature to the
wrong one and have it silently miss most users.

## A planner that will not lie about its own state

The study planner turns a structured intake — courses, available hours, exam
provider's published topic budget — into a strict 14-day grid anchored to the
start of the week, generated by an LLM constrained to structured JSON output.
On top of that sits a persistent AI counselor the student can talk to in
natural language about falling behind or wanting to change the plan. The
counselor never writes to the plan directly. When it commits to a change, the
backend drafts a proposal — a frozen-past, regenerated-future merge of the
plan — and the student has to explicitly apply it before anything changes.
That separation exists because a chat model that can silently rewrite
persistent state will eventually rewrite it based on a misread message, and
the fix has to be structural rather than a prompt asking it to be careful. The
counselor is also fed back the outcome of its own last proposal — applied,
rejected, expired, or still pending — because without that it happily tells a
student it changed a plan they never applied.

## Making the habit itself the product

Underneath both features is a shared incentive layer: a per-user chat streak
counted on local day boundaries, a "shapool" credit balance that meters AI
usage and is topped up through packages, referrals, and streak rewards, and a
Zarinpal-compatible payment flow. Package changes follow one deliberate rule —
renewing the same tier stacks the remaining time, but switching tiers forfeits
it — closing off a cheap-long-plan-funds-a-premium-one loophole rather than
leaving it as an edge case to patch later.

## Native-like web and Android delivery

The web client is a Next.js PWA designed to feel native on mobile: a custom
Service Worker handles installability and cache management, and the UI is
built for thumb-first navigation rather than a desktop site squeezed into a
phone. The frontend stack matches the rest of what I ship — TanStack Query for
server state, Zustand for client state, Zod-validated forms through React Hook
Form, and streamed markdown rendering for chat and study content. Alongside it
is a Trusted Web Activity Android release with FCM push notifications, a
boot-triggered notification scheduler, and three separate in-app billing
gateways (Cafe Bazaar, Myket, and a direct release) behind one billing
interface, since shipping to Iranian Android app stores means there is no
single Play Billing API to rely on.

projects.title: Sakena
projects.summary: A residential-complex management platform for residents, managers, and service staff — a DDD/Clean Architecture Kotlin backend behind a Next.js frontend, covering units, service requests, tasks, payments, and announcements.
highlights: Backend organized as bounded contexts under Clean Architecture, with a strict dependency rule enforced by convention
Three roles — resident, manager, service staff — sharing one API with role-scoped views
Eighteen bounded contexts covering units, service requests, tasks, payments, announcements, chat, and more
Direct messaging between residents and staff with attachment storage
projects.body_md:
## Overview

Sakena is a management platform for residential complexes, built as a team
project for Sharif's Analysis and Software Design course. The premise is
ordinary — apartment buildings need someone to log a leak, a manager needs to
know which units still owe this month's shared costs, a resident wants to
know whether the elevator repair got scheduled — but the system underneath
had to hold up three different users with three different jobs against the
same data.

## Architecture as the actual deliverable

Where most course projects optimize for finishing features, this one treated
the architecture itself as the graded artifact. The Kotlin backend is
organized by bounded context first, then by layer inside each: domain,
application, and infrastructure, with a dependency rule that only points
inward — the domain layer cannot import Spring, JPA, or Jackson, full stop.
Business rules live on the aggregate itself, enforced at construction and
through behavior methods, rather than scattered across services that merely
orchestrate. A small `task` module ships as the deliberate reference
implementation: new bounded contexts are expected to copy its shape rather
than invent a new one, which is what let four people add units, service
requests, payments, announcements, chat, and more without the codebase
drifting into four different styles.

## Three roles, one API

Residents, building managers, and service staff all work through the same
backend with role-scoped permissions rather than separate apps. A manager
manages buildings and units, publishes announcements, and reviews payment
history; a resident files service requests and reads what the manager
posted; a service worker picks up tasks, reports on completed work with cost
and notes attached, and can look back at everything they have finished. That
shared surface is also why the auth layer got early, deliberate attention —
role has to come from the backend's own record of who a user is, never from
a client-side selection, or the three-roles model collapses into "whatever
the frontend claims."

## Frontend

The client is a Next.js app on the same stack I use across these projects —
TanStack Query for server state, Zustand for what is genuinely client state,
Zod schemas driving React Hook Form — because keeping that boundary
consistent is what makes a fast-moving four-person frontend stay readable
instead of accumulating four ad hoc patterns for the same problem.

## What is deliberately not built

Not every backend endpoint has a UI, and that gap is documented rather than
hidden: a generic task CRUD module exists only as the architecture's
reference implementation, not a product feature, so the Tasks screen is
wired to service requests instead. Treating "no UI for this" as a tracked,
intentional decision — not an oversight to quietly leave unfinished — kept
the team's actual scope legible as the project grew.

projects.title: mianGPT
projects.summary: A multi-model AI chat platform with a Django/OpenRouter backend and a streaming Next.js PWA frontend, unifying a web app and a Telegram bot behind one credit-billed API.
highlights: One chat pipeline shared by a web app and a Telegram bot, with two distinct auth surfaces
SSE streaming with per-token billing against a live USD-to-Toman exchange rate
Installable PWA frontend with offline caching and streamed markdown, math, and Mermaid rendering
projects.body_md:
## Overview

mianGPT is a multi-model AI chat product: users pick from a catalog of LLMs
synced live from OpenRouter, chat through a streaming web interface or a
Telegram bot, and pay per token from a wallet billed in Toman. The system
serves two very different clients — a Next.js PWA and a Telegram bot — from
one Django backend, which shaped most of the interesting engineering
decisions.

## One pipeline, two clients

The chat logic — build the message payload, call OpenRouter, stream the
response, persist the assistant message, deduct credit — is written once as a
shared async generator and reused by both the web SSE endpoint and the bot
endpoint. The alternative, duplicating that logic per client, would have meant
two billing implementations quietly drifting apart. Instead the two surfaces
differ only where they have to: the web app authenticates with JWT and speaks
REST plus SSE, while the bot authenticates with a static API key and gets
endpoints shaped to match the schema of the Telegram bot's original SQLite
database, so migrating existing bot users onto the new backend didn't require
touching the bot's own logic.

## Billing on live exchange rates

Wallet balances are held in Toman, but every model's cost from OpenRouter
arrives in USD per token. Billing pulls the USD-to-Toman rate live from the
Bitpin API on a short cache window, with a database-configurable fallback rate
for when that call fails, so a pricing-provider outage degrades to a stale
rate instead of breaking checkout. Per-model prices can be pinned by an admin
independently of what OpenRouter reports, which matters because "pass through
the raw provider cost" and "the price we want to charge" are not always the
same policy, and the system needed room for both.

## Frontend

The web client is a Next.js PWA — a real one, with a generated service worker,
offline caching, and an install prompt, not just a manifest file bolted onto a
normal site. Chat responses stream token-by-token through `streamdown`,
rendering Markdown, LaTeX math, code blocks, and Mermaid diagrams as they
arrive rather than waiting for the full response. State is split the same way
across this codebase as elsewhere: TanStack Query owns server state, Zustand
owns the client-only state, and forms run through React Hook Form with Zod
schemas shared with the API layer.

## Delivery

Both services are containerized and run behind Nginx, with Redis backing OTP
state and API throttling and PostgreSQL as the system of record. Attachment
uploads go through MinIO/S3-compatible storage, and the backend enforces that
an upload has actually finished — non-zero size, `201` returned — before it
can be attached to a message, closing a race where a message sent mid-upload
would silently reference an empty file.

projects.title: L.A. Noire
projects.summary: A noir-styled investigation platform — cases, evidence, complaints, crime scenes, and a React Flow detective board — with RBAC enforced across the React client and the Django API.
projects.role: Auth & payments backend · detective board & rewards frontend (team of 3)
highlights: RBAC enforced symmetrically across routes, UI actions, and API endpoints
Detective board on React Flow for linking cases, evidence, and suspects
Domain coverage for complaints, crime scenes, witness testimony, and tip rewards
CI/CD via GitHub Actions covering build, test, and deploy
projects.body_md:
## Overview

L.A. Noire is a full-stack investigation platform built for the Web Programming
course at Sharif University of Technology, styled after the Rockstar game it
takes its name from. The brief asked for a CRUD application; the goal was
production architecture for a real domain: cases, evidence, complaints, crime
scenes, witness testimony, tip rewards, and a visual detective board.

Built as a team of three. My share was auth and payment on the Django side, and
on the React side the payment flow, detective board, high-priority wanted
suspects, reward claim UI, plus frontend tests.

## Access control as a first-class concern

The core design problem was role-based access control. It is easy to hide a
button in the UI and call that access control — and just as easy to ship a hole
behind it. Here RBAC is enforced in three places that have to agree: route
guards on the frontend, conditional rendering of UI actions, and permission
checks on every Django REST endpoint.

The important part is the asymmetry in how those three are treated. The
frontend checks exist for user experience: they keep people from walking into a
door that will not open. The API checks are the actual boundary. A request that
bypasses the client entirely still has to satisfy the same policy, because the
policy lives on the server and the client only mirrors it.

## Frontend

React with Vite, using TanStack Query for server state and Zustand for the
client state that genuinely is client state — a distinction worth being strict
about, since conflating the two is what turns a state layer into a second,
worse cache.

Forms run through React Hook Form with Zod resolvers, so validation rules are
declared once as schemas and reused for both the form and the typed API
boundary. React Flow (`@xyflow/react`) drives the detective board, where
relationships between cases, evidence, and suspects are explored as a graph
rather than nested tables.

## Backend

Django and Django REST Framework over PostgreSQL, with JWT authentication via
PyJWT, `django-filter` for composable query parameters, and Gunicorn as the
application server. Permissions are attached at the viewset level so a new
endpoint is access-controlled by default rather than by remembering to add a
check.

## Delivery

GitHub Actions runs build, test, and deploy on every push. The whole stack is
containerized, so the environment that runs in development is the environment
that runs in deployment — which removes the class of bug where something works
locally and nowhere else.

projects.title: SharifAC RAG Chatbot
projects.summary: A retrieval-augmented assistant that answers questions about Sharif's academic regulations with citation-backed responses, delivered as a web widget and a Telegram bot.
highlights: Citation-backed answers traced to specific clauses in official documents
Pluggable LLM layer running against either a hosted API or a local model
Observability and evaluation wired in through Langfuse
projects.body_md:
## Overview

Sharif's academic regulations are spread across a pile of PDFs and bylaws that
students are expected to navigate on their own. SharifAC is a machine learning
course project that turns them into something you can ask questions of, and get
answers that cite where they came from.

## Why retrieval, not fine-tuning

The failure mode that matters for this problem is confident invention. A
student asking whether they can drop a course after week six needs the actual
clause, not a plausible-sounding paraphrase of one. That constraint rules out
answering from model weights alone.

Retrieval-augmented generation fits because it inverts the trust relationship:
the authoritative text comes from the document store, and the model's job is
narrowed to phrasing and synthesis. Every answer carries the clauses it was
built from, so a reader can check the source rather than trusting the summary.

## Pipeline

Official PDF and Markdown documents are chunked and embedded into a FAISS
index. A question is embedded, matched against that index, and the top passages
are passed to the model as grounding context alongside the conversation
history. Persistence runs through SQLAlchemy against SQLite in development and
PostgreSQL in deployment.

The LLM integration is deliberately pluggable — OpenAI when a hosted model is
appropriate, Ollama when it needs to run locally. Keeping that boundary behind
an interface meant the retrieval and evaluation work never had to care which
one was active.

## Delivery and evaluation

Two front doors: an embeddable web widget and a Telegram bot, chosen because
they cover how students actually behave on desktop and on mobile without asking
them to learn a new destination.

Langfuse handles observability and evaluation, which matters more than it
sounds — without traces of what was retrieved for a given question, debugging a
bad answer is guesswork. The full system is containerized with Docker.

projects.title: WSS Website
projects.summary: The site for the Winter Seminar Series, the largest event run by Sharif's CE department — frontend and backend features plus a load-performance overhaul.
highlights: SSG and SSR applied per route based on how often each page's data changes
Grouping system, resume upload, and job postings added for organizers
Frontend load performance measurably improved
projects.body_md:
## Overview

The Winter Seminar Series is the largest event the Computer Engineering
department at Sharif runs, and its website carries real traffic in bursts —
quiet for months, then thousands of concurrent visitors when registration
opens. I contributed features across the frontend and backend and led work on
load performance.

## Rendering strategy

The interesting decision was refusing to pick one rendering mode for the whole
site. Next.js supports both static generation and server rendering, and the
right choice differs per route.

Schedule and speaker pages change rarely and are read constantly, so they are
statically generated and served from cache. Registration and dashboard views
depend on who is asking and have to render per request. Treating this as a
per-route decision rather than a global setting is most of where the
performance came from — the pages taking the traffic spike are the ones that
never touch the database.

## Features

I added a grouping system for team registrations, resume upload, and job
posting functionality, each of which had been handled manually by organizers
through spreadsheets in prior years. The frontend uses TanStack Query for
server state, Zustand for client state, and Zod with React Hook Form for
validated multi-step registration flows.

## Backend and deployment

Django and Django REST Framework over PostgreSQL, containerized with Docker and
fronted by Nginx. Nginx does more than proxy here: it terminates TLS, serves
static assets directly without touching the application server, and provides
the buffer that keeps a registration-opening spike from reaching Django all at
once.

projects.title: LakLak
projects.summary: A full product for baby and toddler goods — Django and Kafka backend, React panels, a Docusaurus wiki, and a UI system designed from scratch.
highlights: Kafka used for asynchronous task processing across packaging and shipping
Multiple role-specific panels over one REST API
Custom UI components built to a defined brand identity
projects.body_md:
## Overview

LakLak was the Systems Analysis and Design course project: a full product for
selling and shipping baby and toddler goods, covering the backend, frontend,
documentation, and deployment rather than a single slice of it.

## Why a message queue

The system has several panels — packaging, selling, shipping — that all react
to the same underlying events. An order being placed has to notify packaging,
adjust inventory, and eventually reach shipping.

Doing that synchronously inside the request that creates the order means the
customer waits on work they do not care about, and one slow downstream step
fails the whole order. Kafka decouples them: the order is committed and an
event is published, and each consumer picks up its own work at its own pace. A
consumer being down delays processing rather than dropping the order.

For a course project this is arguably more machinery than the load demands. I
built it that way deliberately — the point was to work through the coordination
problem properly, since getting the boundaries right is the part that does not
transfer from reading about it.

## Frontend and design system

React panels talking to a Django REST Framework API. All the UI elements were
designed and implemented from scratch against a defined brand identity rather
than assembled from a component library — which meant deciding on spacing,
type, and color as a system first, then building components that expressed it.

## Documentation and delivery

A static wiki built with Docusaurus documents the API and the operational
procedures for each panel. Deployment runs on Docker behind Nginx, with GitHub
Actions handling CI/CD. Work was tracked through GitHub Projects following
Scrum practice.

projects.title: Byte Publication Website
projects.summary: Statically exported Next.js site for Byte, Sharif CE's magazine — MDX content, KaTeX math, build-time search, and legacy URLs preserved at byte-mag.ir.
highlights: Rebuilt from Docusaurus to Next.js 16 static export without breaking legacy paths
Build-time content graph — search index, relations, and OG images computed in prebuild
KaTeX math and Shiki code in MDX; Persian-first RTL UI
projects.body_md:
## Overview

Byte is the scientific and cultural magazine of the Computer Engineering
department at Sharif University of Technology. I designed and built its site,
then rebuilt it as a statically exported Next.js app that replaces the earlier
Docusaurus version while keeping every published URL. Live at
[byte-mag.ir](https://byte-mag.ir).

## Why static, still

Articles are written by students and published irregularly. Contributors need
to ship prose without operating a CMS, and the site should not carry a database
for content that changes a few times a term. MDX files in the repo are still
the source of truth — a pull request is the publishing workflow — and
`output: "export"` produces a directory any static host can serve.

## Rebuild

The Docusaurus site worked; it was also hard to evolve. The rebuild keeps the
same content model (issues, articles, blog, workshops, Codenameh, staff) and
adds a build-time search index, Zod-validated frontmatter, issue PDFs on an
external CDN, and a Persian-first RTL UI on Tailwind and shadcn. Counts,
relations, and Open Graph images are generated in `prebuild`, not in the
browser.

## Mathematics

A computer engineering magazine carries real notation. KaTeX renders LaTeX at
build time so equations arrive as text — they scale, follow theme, and stay
visible to search and screen readers — without a client-side math runtime on
every page view.

## Deployment

GitHub Actions builds and deploys on merge to main. Merging a contributor's
article publishes it; there is no separate publish step for anyone to forget.

projects.title: Kanban Board
projects.summary: A drag-and-drop task board in React and TypeScript, using DnDKit for interaction and Zod plus React Hook Form for validated task entry.
highlights: Accessible drag and drop with keyboard support via DnDKit
Optimistic reordering with clean state transitions
Validation schemas shared between form and store
projects.body_md:
## Overview

A Kanban board built for the Web Programming course at Sharif: create boards
and tasks, edit and delete them, and move tasks between columns by dragging.
Small enough to build well rather than merely finish.

## Drag and drop that works without a mouse

Drag and drop is where most task boards quietly become unusable for anyone not
using a pointer. HTML5's native drag events are inconsistent across browsers and
effectively inaccessible from the keyboard.

DnDKit was the right choice specifically because it treats keyboard interaction
as a first-class input rather than an afterthought: a task can be picked up,
moved between columns, and dropped entirely from the keyboard, with the same
state transitions as a pointer drag. It also leaves sensor configuration and
collision detection open, which matters when columns scroll independently.

## State and validation

Zustand holds board state. Reordering applies optimistically — the card moves
the moment you release it, because waiting on anything before showing the
result makes a direct-manipulation interface feel broken.

Task forms use React Hook Form with Zod resolvers, so the shape of a task is
declared once as a schema and drives both the form validation and the types the
store operates on. When the schema changes, everything downstream stops
compiling, which is exactly the behaviour worth having.

## Delivery

Built with Vite and deployed through Vercel's CI/CD. React Hot Toast handles
notifications for the actions that need confirmation.

projects.title: Creepy Gopher
projects.summary: A real-estate management tool in Go pairing a Telegram bot interface with a web crawler — built for speed where Python and Selenium would stall.
highlights: Significantly faster crawling than a typical Python and Selenium approach
Telegram as the entire user interface — no separate app to install
Built during the Quera Software Engineering Bootcamp
projects.body_md:
## Overview

Creepy Gopher searches, filters, and manages property listings. It was built by
a five-person team during the Quera Software Engineering Bootcamp, in Go.

## Why Go for a crawler

Crawling is dominated by waiting — on network responses, on pages rendering, on
rate limits. The work is not CPU-bound, it is concurrency-bound, and how cheaply
a language lets you wait on thousands of things at once decides throughput.

The common approach is Python driving Selenium, where each browser instance is
heavy and concurrency means either threads fighting the GIL or a process pool
that eats memory. Go's goroutines make a few thousand concurrent operations
unremarkable, and the scheduler handles blocking I/O without the caller
structuring anything around it. The result was substantially faster than an
equivalent Python and Selenium implementation.

Playwright handles pages that need real rendering, but only where required —
most listing pages yield to plain HTTP requests and parsing, which is an order
of magnitude cheaper than driving a browser.

## Telegram as the interface

The user interface is a Telegram bot, and this was the right call for the
audience: property hunting happens on a phone, in short bursts. A bot needs no
installation, no account creation, and no notification system of its own, since
Telegram already provides all three.

## Storage and deployment

Listings are normalized into PostgreSQL as they are extracted, so filtering runs
as SQL rather than in application memory. The whole service is containerized
with Docker.

projects.title: Simple Container
projects.summary: A minimal Linux container runtime in C, built on namespaces and cgroups to expose what containerization actually does underneath.
highlights: Process, mount, and network isolation via Linux namespaces
Resource limits enforced through cgroups
Small enough to read end to end in one sitting
projects.body_md:
## Overview

A minimal container runtime written in C for the Operating Systems course. The
goal was not to build something anyone should deploy — it was to remove the
mystery from `docker run` by implementing the parts that matter.

## What a container actually is

The useful realization is that a container is not a thing the kernel has. There
is no container object. There is a normal process that has been lied to about
what it can see, and constrained in what it can consume.

The lying is done by namespaces. A new PID namespace means the process sees
itself as PID 1 and cannot see anything outside. A mount namespace gives it its
own filesystem view, so a `chroot`-style root can be set up without affecting
the host. Network and UTS namespaces isolate interfaces and hostname. Each is a
flag to `clone()`, and together they produce something that looks like a
separate machine from the inside.

The constraining is done by cgroups. Namespaces control visibility but say
nothing about resources — without cgroups an isolated process can still consume
all the memory and CPU on the host. Writing limits into the cgroup filesystem
is what makes isolation meaningful rather than cosmetic.

## Why write it in C

Higher-level languages wrap these syscalls in libraries that make the mechanism
disappear, which defeats the purpose. In C, `clone()`, `mount()`, `pivot_root()`
and the cgroup writes are visible as the syscalls they are, and the ordering
constraints between them — which must happen before the child starts, which
must happen after — are impossible to skip past without understanding them.

## Scope

Deliberately small: process management, namespace setup, root filesystem
switching, and cgroup limits. No image format, no registry, no networking
beyond namespace creation. Those are the parts that make a real runtime large,
and none of them would have taught much beyond what the core already did.

projects.title: RIML Website
